Acronyms: ASHP – Air Source Heat Pump CCHP – Cold Climate Heat Pump MSHP – Mini-Split Heat pump EER – Energy Efficiency Rating SEER – Seasonal Energy Efficiency Rating COP – Coefficient of Performance HSPF – Heating Season Performance Factor UEF – Uniform Energy Factor Through a comparison of the baseline PBC low-income residential building stock with the 16 different upgrade packages, it was found that the upgrade packages that included the ultra-high efficiency heat pump systems with electric back up produced the greatest amount of modeled energy savings (Figure 11). See Figure C-1 in the Appendix C to see a comparison of total electricity consumption of all upgrade packages compared to the baseline. It is important to note that given the high penetration of fully electrified households in Palm Beach County, the comparison of percent of baseline electricity to percent of baseline total energy is very similar. For this analysis, we focused solely on the savings in electricity consumption compared to the baseline. 11 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. Figure 11: Median modeled electricity savings compared to the baseline for low-income households for various upgrade packages Based on Figure 11, there are three main takeaways: • ENERGY STAR (Upgrade 1) and Ultra-high efficiency heat pumps (Upgrade 3) account for a modeled savings in electricity consumption of ~6% and ~20%, respectively, both when applied alone and when applied with envelope and full appliance electrification with efficiency upgrades. • The addition of full appliance electrification with efficiency upgrade package increases modeled savings by 9% when comparing Upgrades 6 and 11 and 8.4% when comparing Upgrades 8 and 13. While all four of these upgrade packages include other HVAC and envelope upgrade measures, there is little interaction between these HVAC and envelope upgrade measures with the upgrades involved in the full appliance electrification with efficiency upgrade package.
